strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: most commonsense benchmarks force a single atomic answer, whereas the proposed benchmark explicitly tests joint plausibility (AND), partial plausibility (OR), and joint implausibility (NEITHER/NOR), preserving a standard MCQ format that makes results directly comparable to existing benchmarks.

The dataset construction pipeline is transparent and well documented: three clearly separated stages (LLM-based generation, LLM-based refinement, deterministic symbolic composition), with all prompt templates provided in the appendix. The deterministic composition stage avoids relying on the LLM for the logical labels themselves, which strengthens label consistency.

The paper includes a human validation study with a clearly described annotation protocol (awareness–consensus framework, guidelines, adjudication procedure), reports inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.49), and separates human-validated (HV) from non-validated (NV) test subsets, allowing readers to assess label-noise sensitivity.

The evaluation is reasonably broad in regimes: zero-shot, 1–3-shot, CoT, and supervised fine-tuning across encoder-only, encoder–decoder, and decoder-only architectures. The fine-tuned results (83–93 F1) are a valuable control showing the task is learnable, supporting the claim that zero-shot failures are inference-time limitations rather than dataset artifacts.

The direct comparison against original CommonsenseQA (Table 3) is a clean and convincing experimental design that supports the central motivation, and the error analysis in Appendix A.7 (single-statement dominance, plausibility collapse, negation inversion) is qualitative but insightful and well illustrated.

Reproducibility materials are largely adequate: exact prompts, decoding parameters, training hyperparameters, annotation guidelines, and model configurations are all reported, and the paper states that data and code will be released.
weaknesses: The headline finding — collapse on NEITHER/NOR — is potentially confounded by label noise in exactly that category. Human validation shows NEITHER/NOR label accuracy is only 73.6% (the lowest of all operators), the validation sample is small (250 questions, 5% of the data), and κ=0.49 is only moderate agreement. Some portion of the observed 6–14% F1 on NEITHER/NOR could reflect systematic label disagreement or GPT-4o-mini mislabeling rather than genuine model reasoning failure; the paper does not quantify this (e.g., accuracy restricted to adjudicated-correct NN items).

Model coverage is limited for a paper claiming to expose 'fundamental reasoning limitations of state-of-the-art systems': only three open-weight decoder-only LLMs (up to 70B), no frontier models (e.g., GPT-4-class, despite GPT-4o-mini being used in construction), and CoT is evaluated for only one model 'due to computational cost.' The abstract's reference to 'reasoning-specialized' models reduces to Entailer-11B, which performs near chance, so claims about reasoning models are under-supported.
The public release URL is a placeholder ('available at and') in the submitted manuscript, undermining the reproducibility claim at review time.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals are reported anywhere, despite per-relation test subsets being modest in size (the HV subset contains only ~250 instances per relation), so several adjacent numbers in the tables (e.g., 0-shot vs. few-shot differences) may not be meaningful.

The paper does not rule out prompt/format artifacts as the source of the NEITHER/NOR failure. Models scoring below chance on NN (7–14 F1) suggests systematic negation inversion, which the error analysis confirms, but there is no ablation with alternative surface realizations (e.g., 'not X or Y', paraphrased negation, or free-form generative answering) to separate operator-grounding failure from answer-format sensitivity.

The MIXED condition is underspecified: it is unclear how uniqueness of the gold option is guaranteed when different operators appear across the four options and the gold is defined as the option whose 'composite plausibility best matches' the question; the construction of unambiguous MIXED labels is not described.

Novelty is moderate: composing answer options with logical operators and diagnosing negation failures echoes established findings (negation brittleness is well documented, e.g., Ettinger 2020 and NLI work), and the paper could more sharply position its contribution relative to negation-focused diagnostics and multi-answer QA work beyond AmbigQA/ProtoQA.

Human validation covers only one language/culture and a small annotator pool; the paper acknowledges cultural bias but the awareness–consensus framing is not exploited in the analysis (e.g., no breakdown of errors by awareness vs. consensus ratings).

strengths: Clear motivation: moving beyond single-answer commonsense evaluation toward compositional plausibility relations (AND/OR/NEITHER-NOR) is a reasonable and well-motivated direction, and the related-work section positions the contribution sensibly between multi-answer QA benchmarks and formal logical reasoning benchmarks.

The dataset construction is largely deterministic in its final stage: symbolic composition over refined atomic options gives a controlled, scalable way to produce ~20k instances while preserving the standard MCQ format, and prompts for all generation stages are included.

The evaluation covers a reasonable spread of paradigms (encoder-only, encoder-decoder, decoder-only LLMs; zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, fine-tuning), with decoding settings and training hyperparameters reported in the appendix.
The error analysis (Section A.7, Table 6) goes beyond aggregate scores and identifies interpretable failure patterns such as single-statement dominance, plausibility collapse, and negation inversion.
A Limitations section is present, and the awareness–consensus annotation framework is a somewhat more principled attempt at capturing socially grounded plausibility than naive binary labeling.
weaknesses: The central claim — that models 'collapse' on negation-based composition — is undermined by the dataset's own label quality on that condition: human validation reports only 73.6% label accuracy for NEITHER/NOR, versus 89–96% for the other operators. Much of the sharp performance drop on NEITHER/NOR could therefore be label noise rather than genuine model failure, and the paper never quantifies how much of the gap survives after restricting to high-confidence labels. This is the single most serious soundness concern.

The semantics of the composed options are underspecified and potentially ambiguous. Under OR ('at least one statement plausible'), an option with two plausible atomics would also satisfy the constraint, yet the gold label design implies exactly one correct option; the paper never proves or explains that exactly one option satisfies the target plausibility semantics per question. Whether the benchmark measures operator understanding or arbitrary distractor conventions is unclear.

Human validation is internally inconsistent and very limited: Section 3 says 250 questions (5%) were validated, then reports 'label accuracy on the adjudicated subset covering 50% of the question-level test split.' It is impossible to reconcile these numbers, and the validated portion of the test set is too small to support strong benchmark-level claims. Cohen's κ = 0.49 (moderate) before adjudication further weakens confidence in the gold labels, which are ultimately produced mostly by GPT-4o-mini self-refinement.

The paper's own evidence suggests possible dataset artifacts rather than inference-time limitations: fine-tuned small models reach 83–93% F1, and in Table 4 the fine-tuned models actually score higher on the non-human-validated (NV) split than the human-validated (HV) split, contradicting the assumption that HV labels are cleaner and suggesting models may learn pipeline-specific labeling patterns.

The main finding has limited novelty: LLM weaknesses on negation are extensively documented in prior work, and the benchmark is essentially CommonsenseQA questions with templated binary compositions of atomic options. No controlled decomposition shows that failures arise from the compositional step rather than from atomic plausibility judgments, which would be needed to substantiate the 'compositional reasoning' framing.

Reproducibility is compromised: the availability statement reads 'The dataset and code are publicly available at and' — both links are empty. Without the dataset, prompts are only partially recoverable and the results cannot be verified.

Evaluation coverage is thin for the claims made: only three decoder-only LLMs (largest is LLaMA-3.3-70B), CoT is evaluated for one small model only due to cost, and there are no significance tests, confidence intervals, or variance estimates anywhere in the paper. Several results are also left unexplained, e.g., few-shot performance on NEITHER/NOR decreasing as shots increase (13.4 → 10.7 for LLaMA-70B), which is counterintuitive and unanalyzed.

The MIXED condition, highlighted as preventing operator-specific shortcuts, is itself only loosely defined ('operators are randomly assigned across options'), and it is unclear what the gold answer means when different operators co-occur within one question's option set.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly positioned: reframing commonsense QA as logical composition over plausibility judgments (AND/OR/NEITHER-NOR) addresses a genuine gap left by single-answer benchmarks, and the paper is honest that the operators are 'plausibility-level' constructs rather than strict propositional logic.

The construction pipeline is sensibly designed, combining LLM-based generation and refinement with a deterministic symbolic composition step, which makes the operator labels internally consistent by construction rather than another source of annotation subjectivity.

Human validation follows a principled framework (awareness-consensus from Whiting and Watts 2024) with documented guidelines (Appendix A.4), adjudication procedures, and reporting of inter-annotator agreement.

The evaluation covers a reasonable spread of paradigms (encoder-only, encoder-decoder, decoder-only LLMs; zero/few-shot, CoT, fine-tuning), includes a stratified MIXED condition that guards against operator-pattern exploitation, and provides a useful comparison against the original CommonsenseQA (Table 3).

The error analysis (Appendix A.7) goes beyond aggregate numbers, identifying concrete and interpretable failure modes (single-statement dominance, plausibility collapse, negation inversion) that make the claimed model limitations tangible.

The main finding — sharp collapse on negation-based compositions (13-14% F1, below chance) versus decent conjunctive performance — is striking, consistent across three LLM families, and plausibly consequential for how the community interprets CommonsenseQA-style scores.
weaknesses: Label noise on the hardest subset undermines the central claim: the paper reports only 73.6% human label accuracy for NEITHER/NOR, exactly the relation where models 'collapse'. Some portion of the negation failure could reflect ambiguous or contested gold labels rather than model inability; the paper does not disentangle these (e.g., no per-instance agreement filtering or analysis restricted to high-consensus items).

Human validation coverage is very thin and internally inconsistent: 250 questions (5% of Stage 2) with two annotators is described, but the validation subset is later said to cover '50% of the question-level test split' defined after Stage 2 — the relationship between these numbers is never clarified, and the test-set HV/NV distinction is left under-specified.

Reproducibility is compromised at a Bearer [REDACTED] the abstract states the dataset and code are 'publicly available at [blank] and [blank]' — the URLs are missing from the manuscript. For a resource paper, this is a serious omission.

Ensuring a unique correct answer under each operator is not explained. Under OR ('at least one statement plausible'), a distractor composed of one plausible and one implausible clause could be nearly as defensible as the gold option; the paper does not describe constraints guaranteeing that only one option satisfies the operator semantics, which directly threatens label validity for OR and MIXED.

Model coverage is narrower than the abstract suggests: 'reasoning-specialized' evaluation amounts to Entailer-11B (an older, weak-performing model at 3-24 F1), CoT is only run on one 8B model, and no modern reasoning models (e.g., R1-class) or larger frontier models beyond LLaMA-70B are tested, limiting the strength of the 'fundamental limitations' claim.

The inference that fine-tuned success (83-93 F1) shows zero/few-shot failures are 'inference-time limitations rather than dataset artifacts' is not fully supported: fine-tuned models could be learning surface-level operator/format heuristics on a deterministic composition scheme, and no probing or held-out operator generalization is provided to rule this out.

Few-shot results are anomalous and under-examined: NN performance often drops with more shots (e.g., LLaMA-8B from 13.1 to 6.1), suggesting prompt sensitivity or format artifacts, and the fixed 3-example prompt reused across all questions raises mild contamination-style concerns; these instabilities are reported but not analyzed.
Annotation quality controls are thin: κ = 0.49 is only moderate, and no annotator demographics, expertise, or compensation details are reported despite the socially-grounded framing of the benchmark.

The analysis is largely single-model for the headline comparison (Table 3 uses only LLaMA-3.1-8B); showing the CommonsenseQA-to-composition drop generalizes across models would substantially strengthen the motivation.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated task design: reframing commonsense MCQ as plausibility-level logical composition (AND/OR/NEITHER-NOR) over pairs of atomic answers is a sensible and relatively novel angle that preserves standard benchmark format while testing compositional reasoning.

Well-documented, transparent construction pipeline: the three-stage procedure (LLM generation, LLM refinement, deterministic symbolic composition) is described in detail, with prompt templates provided in the appendix, supporting reproducibility.

Human validation with reasonable rigor: two annotators plus adjudication, awareness–consensus framework grounded in Whiting & Watts (2024), and high inter-annotator agreement (Gwet's AC2 of 0.84/0.91), with annotation guidelines reported.

Broad empirical coverage: encoder, encoder–decoder, open-weight decoder LLMs (7B–70B), and closed-source models, across zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, and fine-tuning regimes, with stratified splits and both accuracy and macro-F1.

Strong analysis beyond headline numbers: a decomposition analysis separating atomic plausibility estimation, operator grounding, and distractor competition, plus a qualitative error taxonomy (single-statement dominance, negation inversion, plausibility dominance) that substantiates the claim that difficulty arises from interaction of factors rather than a single failure mode.

Useful negative control: comparison showing LLaMA-3.1-8B's sharp drop from 72.2% on CommonsenseQA to 13.9% on NEITHER/NOR composites directly supports the paper's central claim that single-answer benchmarks overestimate compositional ability.
Dataset and code publicly released; diversity analysis (Distinct-2, semantic diversity) addresses generation-collapse concerns.
weaknesses: Label noise is concentrated precisely on the headline finding: reported label accuracy for NEITHER/NOR is only 73.6%, yet the paper's central empirical claim is a collapse on NEITHER/NOR. Some of the near-random zero-shot F1 (~13%, below the ~25% chance level for 4 options) could partly reflect noisy or ambiguous gold labels rather than pure model failure; a sensitivity analysis on the validated subset helps, but this tension is not fully resolved.

Human validation covers only 250 of 4,999 questions (~50% of the 500-question test source), so the majority of test instances, including many NEITHER/NOR items, rest on LLM-generated and LLM-refined labels, raising circularity concerns since GPT-4o-mini both generates and filters the data.

The human evaluation is far too small to support its conclusions: 10 examples per condition yields accuracies of 0.90/0.70/0.70/0.90 with enormous uncertainty; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported anywhere in the paper.

Potential task shortcuts and artifacts are underexplored: in operator-specific conditions all options share the operator, so the task may reduce to comparing atomic plausibility of pairs; the very low NEITHER/NOR scores may partly reflect surface-format misunderstanding of 'NEITHER...NOR' as an answer string rather than genuine reasoning failure, and the paper does not test e.g. paraphrased negation to disambiguate.

Novelty is moderate: the combination of multiple valid answers (AmbigQA, ProtoQA), logical operator composition (LogiQA, ReClor, COM2), and CommonsenseQA-style data is acknowledged in related work, and the delta of the proposed formulation over these lines could be articulated more sharply.

Fine-tuned models reach 83–95% F1, indicating the benchmark is largely learnable; the paper interprets this as evidence the failures are inference-time limitations, but it does not analyze what fine-tuned models learn (e.g., operator-conditional heuristics), leaving the 'reasoning vs. shortcut' question open.

Annotator details are missing (who the annotators were, expertise, compensation, demographics), and there is no discussion of annotator disagreement on NEITHER/NOR items specifically, where accuracy is weakest.

Minor presentation issues: CoT is claimed in the abstract but evaluated only for one model with weak results; Gemini-3-Flash-Preview lacks a citation; footnotes for dataset/code links are empty in the PDF; some inconsistencies between main-text claims and appendix results (e.g., NN F1 across subsets).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: moving beyond single-answer commonsense evaluation toward compositional plausibility judgments (AND/OR/NEITHER-NOR) is a legitimate angle, and the paper positions itself well against AMBIGQA, ProtoQA, and deductive-logic benchmarks.

The construction pipeline is transparently documented: the three-stage process (candidate generation, refinement, deterministic symbolic composition) is described in detail, with prompt templates provided in the appendix, and dataset/code are stated to be publicly released, supporting reproducibility.

The evaluation is broad, covering encoder-only, encoder-decoder, open-weight decoder-only, and closed-source models under zero-shot, few-shot, CoT, and fine-tuning regimes, with stratified splits and both accuracy and macro-F1 reported.

The decomposition analysis (atomic plausibility vs. operator verification vs. distractor competition) and the qualitative error analysis (single-statement dominance, negation inversion) add analytic depth beyond a simple leaderboard, and the fine-tuned results (83–95% F1) usefully show the task is learnable.
Inter-annotator agreement statistics (Gwet's AC2 = 0.84/0.91) and diversity metrics are reported, which is more careful than many LLM-generated benchmarks.
weaknesses: The central claim — that models 'collapse' on NEITHER/NOR — is undermined by the paper's own evidence that the NEITHER/NOR portion of the data is noisy or ambiguous: gold-label accuracy for NEITHER/NOR is only 73.6%, human accuracy on NEITHER/NOR is 0.70 (and only 0.70 on OR as well), and the human study uses just 10 examples per condition, far too small to establish that the benchmark is reliably solvable by humans while systematically hard for models.

Human validation covers only 250 of 4,999 questions (50% of a 500-question test set, itself only ~10% of the data); the remaining ~19,700 instances rest entirely on GPT-4o-mini self-generated and self-refined labels, so the validity of the training/development data and much of the test data is unverified.

The operator semantics are under-specified. With 'plausibility-level' rather than strict propositional operators, OR questions with multiple plausible atomic answers may admit multiple correct options, and the determinism of the symbolic composition (Stage 3) inherits whatever errors the LLM labeling makes — the paper does not fully resolve how unique gold answers are guaranteed.

The headline finding that LLMs struggle with negation is well documented in prior work (e.g., Ettinger 2020; Geiger et al. 2020, both cited by the authors), so the conceptual novelty is limited; the contribution is mostly a new dataset rather than a new insight.

Within operator-specific conditions, all four options share the same operator, so the task reduces largely to ranking statement plausibility within a fixed operator frame — the reported near-chance LLaMA-8B F1 (13.1) on NEITHER/NOR may reflect prompt/format degeneracy rather than a reasoning deficit, and the paper does not rule this out.

There is a circularity risk: options are generated and refined by GPT-4o-mini, and the near-miss distractors are explicitly designed around subtle violations; fine-tuned models reaching 83–95% could equally indicate learnable annotation artifacts rather than genuine logical composition, and the paper's interpretation ('task is learnable') is not critically examined.
Evaluation of proprietary models (Gemini variants) with zero-shot only, with no contamination analysis, and no significance testing or variance estimates anywhere in the results.

Some reported numbers are internally hard to reconcile (e.g., label accuracy figures are reported 'on the adjudicated dataset' without a clear reference standard), and the writing occasionally overstates conclusions relative to the evidence (e.g., 'exposes fundamental reasoning limitations').
